831.quote_or_event: “As a man for the sake of one Kâkinî (risks and) loses a thousand (Kârshâpanas), or as the king lost his kingdom (and life) by eating a mango-fruit which he was strictly forbidden (by his physician)”
831.explanation: In the 'Parable of the Ram' Mahāvīra's teaching shows the fool trading something vast for a trifle, like a man who loses a thousand coins for a single small one, or a king who loses his kingdom for a forbidden mango.
831.tie_back: Valluvar defines folly as grasping what harms you and letting real gain slip away; the Uttarādhyayana's man who loses a thousand coins for one small coin shows that very trade.
831._accuracy_note: Verified on sacred-texts.com (italic markup in 'Kârshâpanas' removed). The verse is the first half of a comparison completed in v. 12 (human pleasures against divine ones), but the image of a fool swapping great gain for small loss matches the Kural closely.

832.quote_or_event: “The presumptuously saying, We are those who will do what should not be done, and the deferring and putting aside that which ought to be done at once, verily these two things will cause affliction instantly, even to ascetics, who have renounced the pleasures of the domestic state.”
832.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār names two ruinous habits: boldly taking up what should not be done, and putting off what should be done at once, and it says they bring trouble even to renunciants.
832.tie_back: Valluvar calls the greatest folly a fond desire for deeds unfitting for oneself; the Nālaṭiyār likewise puts eagerness to do 'what should not be done' first among the habits that bring swift affliction.
832.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 24 ('Improper Friendship'), st. 5 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
832._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org. A Tamil Jain text; it closely matches the moral reading of the Kural (choosing forbidden acts), though it adds a second fault, procrastination, which the Kural does not mention.

833.quote_or_event: “If he is frequently angry; if he perseveres in his wrath; if he spurns friendly advice; if he is proud of his learning; if he finds fault with others; if he is angry even with friends; if he speaks evil even of a good friend behind his back; if he is positive in his assertions; if he is malicious, egoistical, greedy, without self-discipline; if he does not share with others; if he is always unkind: then he is called ill-behaved.”
833.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana lists the marks of an 'ill-behaved' monk, a whole disposition of anger, ingratitude, greed and unkindness that keeps him from Nirvāṇa.
833.tie_back: Valluvar sketches the fool through a catalogue of lacks (no shame, no seeking, no affection, no care); the Uttarādhyayana similarly defines the ill-behaved by a list of traits, including lacking kindness and not sharing with others.
833._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com. It matches the Kural's catalogue form and its 'lovelessness', but it describes an undisciplined monk and leaves out the Kural's specific points about shamelessness and not seeking what is worth seeking.

834.quote_or_event: “Acknowledging the truth about bondage and liberation, but talking only, not acting (in accordance with these tenets), they seek comfort for themselves in mighty words. Clever talking will not work salvation; how should philosophical instruction do it? Fools, though sinking lower and lower through their sins, believe themselves to be wise men.”
834.explanation: In 'The False Ascetic' Mahāvīra rebukes those who know and speak the doctrine but do not live by it, calling them fools who think themselves wise.
834.tie_back: Valluvar says no fool is greater than one who has studied, understood and taught, yet does not himself conform; the Uttarādhyayana likewise calls those who talk the truth without acting on it 'fools' who sink while believing themselves wise.
834._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com. A near one-to-one match from canonical scripture: knowing and talking the doctrine without self-restraint is named as folly.

835.quote_or_event: “The capital is human life, the gain is heaven; through the loss of that capital man must be born as a denizen of hell or a brute animal. ... Having once forfeited them, he will have to endure these two states of misery; it will be difficult for him to attain an upward course for a long time to come.”
835.explanation: Mahāvīra's parable of the three merchants treats a human life as capital; the fool who squanders it in one life falls into hell or animal birth and struggles for a very long time to rise again.
835.tie_back: Valluvar says the fool in one birth makes the hell he will sink into for seven; the Uttarādhyayana likewise has one wasted human life bring rebirth in hell from which an 'upward course' is hard to win 'for a long time to come'.
835._accuracy_note: Verified on sacred-texts.com; v. 17 is left out (marked by the ellipsis), and Jacobi's '(viz. birth as a man or a god)' footnote marker after 'upward course' is dropped. A strong fit with the traditional eschatological reading of the Kural, though Jainism counts long ages of rebirth rather than 'seven births'.

836.quote_or_event: “As the burglar caught in the breach of the wall perishes by the work the sinner himself had executed, thus people in this life and the next cannot escape the effect of their own actions.”
836.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana pictures a burglar trapped and crushed in the very hole he dug, as an image of how a person's own deeds catch and bind him.
836.tie_back: Valluvar says the fool who takes up work he does not understand not only fails but puts himself in fetters; the Uttarādhyayana's burglar caught in his own breach is likewise undone by his own handiwork.
836._accuracy_note: Verified on sacred-texts.com (footnote marker removed). It shares the image of being trapped by one's own work, but it is about karmic retribution for sin rather than incompetence in a task, so the fit is partial.

837.quote_or_event: “The bat will not go to the rough-stemmed wood-apple tree, though near and fruitful. So the riches of those who, though they be very near to one, have no greatness of soul, have not the excellence of being considered as profitable.”
837.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār says the wealth of small-souled people is of no use even to those closest to them, like a fruitful tree that the bat will not visit.
837.tie_back: Valluvar says that when a fool gets great wealth his own people go hungry; the Nālaṭiyār similarly observes that riches in the hands of those without greatness of soul do nothing for those near them.
837.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 27 ('Riches without goodness'), st. 1 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
837._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org. A Tamil Jain text giving only a partial parallel: it shares the point that those nearby gain nothing, but lacks the Kural's contrast with strangers who feast.

838.quote_or_event: “Wealth will not protect a careless man in this world and the next. Though he had seen the right way, he does not see it, even as one in the dark whose lamp has suddenly been put out.”
838.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana says possessions do not save the heedless person; his judgment goes dark, as when a lamp is suddenly put out.
838.tie_back: Valluvar compares a fool who gets possessions to a madman who is also drunk; the Uttarādhyayana likewise shows wealth failing the heedless man and his sight of the right way vanishing.
838._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com. A next-best match: it links wealth with loss of judgment, but its image is darkness rather than double intoxication, and it concerns spiritual carelessness, not the fool's behaviour with sudden riches.

839.quote_or_event: “This is the road to it: to serve the Gurus and the old (teachers), to avoid throughout foolish people, to apply oneself earnestly to study, and to ponder zealously on the meaning of the Sûtras.”
839.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana counts keeping clear of foolish people among the steps on the road to final deliverance.
839.tie_back: Valluvar jokes that friendship with fools is sweet because parting from them costs nothing; the Uttarādhyayana states the same lesson plainly, that fools are to be avoided altogether.
839._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com. It shares the Kural's verdict on fools' company but has none of its irony about painless parting, so it is a partial match.

840.quote_or_event: “If one who has grown up in ignorance enter the assembly of the excellent in learning, in the earth, and sits down, it will be like the sitting down of a dog; and though, not remaining quiet, he should say anything, it will be like the barking of a dog.”
840.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār mocks the ignorant man who enters a gathering of the learned: his sitting there is like a dog's, and his speech is like barking.
840.tie_back: Valluvar compares a fool entering the assembly of the wise to putting unwashed feet on a clean bed; the Nālaṭiyār uses an equally earthy image for the same intrusion, a dog sitting and barking among the learned.
840.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 26 ('The want of understanding'), st. 4 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
840._accuracy_note: Verified on wisdomlib.org (the online text's typo 'ofa dog' is corrected to 'of a dog'). A Tamil Jain text; it is a near one-to-one parallel in situation and tone, and was used because no canonical verse fits as closely.
